title: AI beyond the hype: How business leaders should think about AI
gist: Oxford Economics CEO Innes McFee argues AI's macro productivity impact remains modest (~3% over ten years) because adoption is still narrow and low-value, and pushes back on hype by insisting trusted data, methodology and human original insight become more valuable, not less, as AI spreads.

themes.theme: AI's economy-wide productivity payoff is smaller and slower than the hype suggests

insights.claim: Oxford Economics CEO Innes McFee holds to an estimate of roughly 3% productivity growth from AI over ten years, well below more bullish economist projections, and says recent evidence continues to support that lower number rather than the bigger claims.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Investors pricing AI-driven productivity booms into equity multiples or GDP forecasts should discount aggressive productivity-growth narratives; a credible economist's central case is far more muted.
insights.quote: Yes. If anything, the evidence over the last couple of months has borne that out.
insights.locator: AI's economic impact and the way forward

insights.claim: Meaningful economy-wide AI productivity gains require three conditions to hold simultaneously: adoption must be widespread, AI must be applied to high-value work, and it must automate a substantial share of those activities -- and none of these conditions is yet satisfied.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete checklist for judging when an AI productivity story is actually investable versus still aspirational -- track adoption breadth, task value, and automation depth together, not any single metric.
insights.quote: For AI to generate meaningful economy-wide productivity gains, three things need to happen simultaneously.
insights.locator: For AI to generate meaningful economy-wide productivity gains

insights.claim: Current AI adoption inside organisations is patchy across industries and concentrated on a small share of tasks that tend to be lower value-add, which explains why usage growth has not yet translated into a productivity shift.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Explains the disconnect between high reported AI adoption rates and flat aggregate productivity data -- adoption breadth alone is not the signal to watch, task value is.
insights.quote: most organisations are using AI for a relatively small proportion of tasks, and those tasks tend to be lower value-add

insights.claim: The real economic upside from AI arrives once it stops being an individual productivity tool for drafting emails or summarising reports and instead gets embedded across end-to-end business workflows automating multiple connected tasks.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Points investors toward workflow-automation and enterprise-process vendors rather than consumer chatbot usage metrics as the leading indicator of scalable AI economic value.
insights.quote: Once AI becomes part of an end-to-end workflow, automating multiple connected tasks, it becomes much more scalable.
insights.locator: I think the biggest change will come when AI moves beyond being a tool

themes.theme: Data quality and human expertise get more valuable, not less, as AI spreads

insights.claim: Against the narrative that AI commoditizes expertise, Innes McFee argues trusted data, rigorous methodology and original analysis become more valuable, not less, in an AI-saturated world because AI makes information easier to access but does not improve its underlying quality.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Supports a bull case for data/analytics providers and research houses with proprietary, well-governed datasets as AI-era winners, rather than AI compressing their pricing power.
insights.quote: trusted data, rigorous methodology and original analysis will only become even more valuable in an AI world, not less.
insights.locator: That's why I think trusted data, rigorous methodology

insights.claim: AI is very good at assimilating huge amounts of information but is not good at original insight, and McFee believes it will be a long time, if ever, before it gets there -- implying AI augments rather than replaces analysts and researchers.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A useful filter for evaluating AI-replaces-knowledge-workers narratives: watch for AI displacing synthesis/summarization tasks while original-insight roles (research, strategy, forecasting) remain human-anchored and defensible.
insights.quote: It is very good at assimilating huge amounts of information. But it is not good at original insight, at least not yet. I think it will be a long time, if ever, before it gets there.
insights.locator: AI is an incredibly powerful tool

insights.claim: If an organisation's internal data isn't built on consistent definitions and methodologies, AI outputs generated from it rest on unreliable foundations, so data governance is a prerequisite for trustworthy AI-driven decisions, not an afterthought.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: For companies rushing to point AI at messy internal data, this flags a hidden cost center -- data cleanup and standardisation -- that must precede any productivity payoff, a useful diligence question for AI-transformation vendors and their clients.
insights.quote: if the underlying data isn’t built on consistent definitions and methodologies, how do you know the foundations aren’t made of sand?
insights.locator: Many organisations are now turning AI towards their own internal data

themes.theme: How leaders should operationalize AI: problem-first, few bets done well

insights.claim: Business leaders should start AI initiatives from the business problem rather than the technology, replacing the question 'How do we use AI?' with 'Where could AI genuinely improve a decision, solve a problem, or strengthen an existing workflow?'
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A practical screen for evaluating corporate AI strategies and vendor pitches -- discount initiatives framed around deploying a technology and favor ones anchored to a specific workflow or decision bottleneck.
insights.quote: A better question is " Where could AI genuinely improve a decision, solve a problem or strengthen an existing workflow?"
insights.locator: I think they should start with the business problem

insights.claim: Oxford Economics is exposing its research and data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) so client organisations can pull it directly into their own AI environments instead of logging into Oxford Economics' systems, and McFee expects this kind of embedded-access model to be where a great deal of value is created over the next few years.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Signals a broader shift for B2B data/research vendors from portal-based delivery to protocol-level integration (MCP) as the next competitive battleground -- worth tracking which providers ship MCP endpoints first.
insights.quote: Rather than asking users to come into our systems, they allow organisations to access our research, data directly through their own AI environments.
insights.locator: Capabilities such as the Model Context Protocol

insights.claim: Organisations should concentrate effort on a small number of AI use cases executed properly rather than spreading across many initiatives left only partially finished, since a thousand 60%-complete projects deliver no client benefit despite the work involved.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A concentration-over-diversification heuristic for evaluating corporate AI roadmaps -- firms announcing dozens of parallel AI pilots may be a red flag versus firms shipping a few fully realised use cases.
insights.quote: there is no point pursuing a thousand initiatives that are all 60% complete if our clients never see the benefit.
insights.locator: At Oxford Economics, I always say there is no point pursuing a thousand initiatives

themes.theme: Reliability and transparency as the price of deploying AI

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' economists spent months training and testing its AskOE AI assistant before release -- reviewing outputs, repeating questions, challenging responses and flagging potentially misleading answers -- and deliberately gave up some functionality to keep client-facing outputs accurate and grounded in the firm's research.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A concrete internal case study of the cost/reliability tradeoff in enterprise AI deployment -- useful benchmark for due diligence on how rigorously other vendors have validated their AI products before shipping.
insights.quote: We were prepared to give up some functionality to ensure that the information clients received was accurate and grounded in our research.
insights.locator: Our experience developing AskOE reinforced that

insights.claim: Organisations deploying AI need to be transparent about how the technology is being used, where its limits lie, and what has been done to make outputs reliable, because more functionality is not automatically better if users cannot trust the output.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Sets a governance bar investors can use to assess enterprise AI vendors and adopters -- transparency about limitations, not feature breadth, is the differentiator that protects trust and downstream liability.
insights.quote: More functionality is not automatically better if users cannot rely on the output.
insights.locator: They need to be transparent about how the technology is being used
